common_name: Codd's Agapanthus (Highveld Grassland Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring or set out container plants into well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun; Codd's agapanthus comes from frosty, summer-rainfall highveld grasslands of the Mpumalanga and Limpopo escarpment, so it tolerates colder winters than the evergreen coastal species once established.

directions: Codd's agapanthus is a lesser-grown deciduous species from the frost-prone grasslands of South Africa's eastern escarpment, dying back completely each winter and resprouting narrow, grass-like leaves in spring. Flower scapes carry rounded umbels of pale lilac-blue, upward-facing blooms in mid to late summer, somewhat more erect than the nodding habit of many other agapanthus species. Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun, and allow clumps to become slightly congested before dividing, since flowering improves with a little crowding. Its grassland origin makes it a good candidate for naturalistic prairie-style plantings alongside other summer-blooming perennials in zones where winter frost rules out the evergreen species.
sources: South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) PlantZAfrica

common_name: Walsh's Agapanthus (Dwarf Cliff-Dwelling Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun; Walsh's agapanthus naturally grows rooted in crevices of sandstone cliffs in the Drakensberg, so it needs far less water and richness than garden agapanthus species.

directions: Walsh's agapanthus is a dwarf, slow-growing species found wedged into sandstone cliff crevices in the Drakensberg mountains, forming small tufts of narrow, almost grass-fine leaves. Nodding, pale lilac to near-white tubular flowers appear in small umbels on short stems in summer, far more delicate than the bold heads of common garden agapanthus. Grow in a gritty, fast-draining mix in a rock garden, raised bed, or trough where its roots can stay dry between waterings, since it is intolerant of wet, heavy soils. Protect from hard freezes in colder zones by growing in a container that can be moved under cover, as this species is less cold-hardy than the deciduous grassland agapanthus species.
sources: South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) PlantZAfrica

common_name: Lydenburg Agapanthus (Robust Late-Blooming Deep Violet-Blue Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Lydenburg is a wild-collected selection named for the Mpumalanga escarpment district where it was found, valued by breeders and collectors for its vigor and late flowering.

directions: Lydenburg is a robust, clump-forming selection named for the district of South Africa's Mpumalanga escarpment where it was originally collected, prized by agapanthus collectors and breeders for its vigor and unusually late summer bloom period, which extends the agapanthus season after earlier cultivars have finished. Tall, sturdy scapes carry large umbels of deep violet-blue flowers well above the strap-shaped evergreen foliage. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, and avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which pushes leafy growth at the expense of bloom. Its large, mature clump size and strong constitution make it well suited to back-of-border plantings and mass displays where big, dependable flower heads are wanted late in the season.

common_name: Albidus Bell Agapanthus (White-Flowered Deciduous Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring or plant container-grown plants in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Albidus is a white-flowered selection of the cold-hardy, deciduous bell agapanthus and shares its parent species' ability to survive into zone 6.

directions: Albidus is a pure white-flowered form of the deciduous bell agapanthus, bearing the same rounded umbels of pendant, bell-shaped flowers as the species but in clear white rather than blue-violet, held on upright scapes above narrow strap leaves. Like its parent species it dies back completely to the ground each winter, a trait that contributes to its exceptional cold hardiness among agapanthus, surviving reliably into zone 6. Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and resist dividing too often, since both foliage fullness and flower count build over two to three undisturbed seasons. Pair with the blue-flowered species or other dark-colored summer perennials for strong color contrast in the mixed border.

common_name: Flore Pleno Agapanthus (Double-Flowered White Lily of the Nile)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Flore Pleno is a long-cultivated double-flowered form of evergreen agapanthus grown chiefly for its fully packed, rounded flower heads.

directions: Flore Pleno is an old, long-cultivated double-flowered selection of evergreen agapanthus, its individual blooms packed with extra petal-like segments so that each flower reads as a tight white rosette rather than the usual open funnel shape, giving the summer umbels a denser, more textured appearance than single-flowered forms. Because it sets little to no seed, all of its energy goes into the long-lasting flower display, and spent scapes can be left to enjoy the blooms even longer than single kinds. Grow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates, and divide only when clumps become overcrowded, since flowering is heaviest on well-established plants. Its clean white color and unusual double form make it a conversation-piece addition to borders otherwise planted with the common blue species.

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; this is the original coastal Chilean and Peruvian species that gave the genus its name, and it needs a drier, more Mediterranean-type winter than most garden Peruvian lily hybrids.

directions: This is the historically important species that gave the genus Alstroemeria its name, collected along the coast of Chile and Peru and among the first Peruvian lilies grown in European gardens in the eighteenth century. Flowers are pale lilac-pink to white with a deep maroon-purple blotched throat on the two upper petals, carried in small loose clusters on wiry stems close to the clump of narrow, grayish leaves. Plant tuberous roots in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun, keeping this coastal-desert species on the dry side, especially during its summer dormancy, since it is far less tolerant of wet soil than many modern hybrid Peruvian lilies. Its tender nature and dislike of humid, wet conditions make it best suited to rock gardens, raised beds, or containers in mild, dry-summer climates rather than the humid Gulf South border.

common_name: Chilean Alstroemeria (Red-and-Gold Spotted Peruvian Lily Species)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; this central Chilean woodland-edge species is taller and more vigorous than many garden Peruvian lily hybrids.

directions: Native to woodland edges and scrub of central Chile, this species bears deep red to crimson-pink flowers whose two upper petals are boldly streaked and spotted with yellow and purple-brown, a strongly marked bicolor pattern typical of the wild Chilean Peruvian lilies. It grows taller and more upright than many dwarf garden hybrids, sending up wiry stems topped with loose, few-flowered clusters from late spring into summer. Plant tuberous roots in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, and allow the clump to spread undisturbed, since flowering improves as the colony matures. Like other Chilean Peruvian lily species, it goes dormant in the heat of summer and should be kept drier during that rest period.

common_name: Magnificent Alstroemeria (Purple-and-Cream Chilean Peruvian Lily Species)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring in well-drained, gritty soil in full sun to partial shade; this Chilean species has contributed its bold flower color to Peruvian lily breeding programs.

directions: A wild Chilean species valued by breeders for its richly colored flowers, which range through shades of violet-purple and pink with the upper petals boldly streaked in cream and marked with dark flecking, a dramatic combination among the Peruvian lily species. Clumps send up slender stems carrying loose, open clusters of flowers in late spring and early summer above narrow, twisted leaves typical of the genus. Grow in well-drained, somewhat gritty soil in full sun to partial shade, mimicking the rocky slopes and scrubland of its native central Chile, and keep it on the drier side through its summer dormancy. As a species rather than a bred hybrid, flower color and size can vary somewhat between individual plants grown from seed or wild-collected stock.

common_name: Smith's Parish Rose (Bermuda Mystery China Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Smith's Parish is a 'found rose' of unknown origin identified growing in Bermuda and named for the parish where it was rediscovered, valued for heat tolerance and near-continuous bloom.

directions: Smith's Parish is one of several 'mystery roses' of Bermuda whose original European or Chinese names were lost, rediscovered by rose researchers growing in old gardens and cemeteries and given a working name based on the parish where the surviving plant was found. It forms a tall, somewhat lax China-type shrub that can be trained as a short climber, producing clusters of fragrant, double, deep pink to cherry-red blooms in continuous flushes through the warm season. Like other Bermuda found roses, it thrives in hot, humid, salt-air conditions that cause many modern roses to struggle, and it shows strong resistance to blackspot and other fungal disease without spraying. Give it a sunny spot with room to arch and spread, and prune lightly after main flushes rather than hard, since it blooms on a framework of older wood as well as new growth.
sources: Help Me Find Roses — historical registry
American Rose Society — China Rose Class Descriptions

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Belfield is a 'found rose' identified growing on an old Bermuda property and named for the estate where it survived, valued for its heat tolerance and disease resistance.

directions: Belfield is another of the unidentified 'mystery roses' of Bermuda, old China-type cultivars whose original names were lost over generations of cultivation and which rose researchers have catalogued under the name of the property or garden where each surviving specimen was rediscovered. It grows as a dense, rounded China-type shrub bearing clusters of double, soft pink blooms over a long warm-season bloom period, with the glossy, disease-resistant foliage typical of old China roses. As with other Bermuda roses, it has proven itself over generations in a hot, humid, salt-laden climate that is hard on many modern roses, needing no fungicide program to stay healthy. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and prune lightly to shape rather than cutting hard, since old wood continues to flower well in this class of rose.
sources: Help Me Find Roses — historical registry
American Rose Society — China Rose Class Descriptions

common_name: Indica Major Rose (Historic Large-Flowered China Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Indica Major is a historic nineteenth-century China rose once grown extensively for cut flowers and as understock, larger in flower and growth than the related Old Blush.

directions: Indica Major is a historic China rose distinct from the similar but smaller-flowered Old Blush, long grown in nineteenth-century gardens and glasshouses for its larger, loosely double, pale pink blooms that deepen in color with cooler weather and age. It was once widely used in the cut-flower and nursery trade, valued for its vigor and reliable repeat bloom from spring through frost in mild climates. The bush grows larger and more vigorously than many other old China roses, with glossy, reddish-tinted new foliage characteristic of the class. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, and prune lightly in late winter to remove dead or crowded growth, since it flowers best on an open, well-ventilated framework of older wood.
sources: Help Me Find Roses — historical registry
The Old Rose Advisor (Brent C. Dickerson)
American Rose Society — China Rose Class Descriptions

common_name: Rival de Paestum Rose (Antique White China-Tea Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall; Rival de Paestum is an 1841 French antique China-tea rose grown for its creamy white, repeat-flowering blooms tinged pink in cool weather.

directions: Rival de Paestum is an antique French China-tea rose bred in the first half of the nineteenth century, prized for its creamy white, double flowers that take on a delicate blush-pink tint at the petal edges during cool spring and fall weather. It blooms in repeated flushes from spring through frost in mild climates, holding its flowers well despite their pale color, which can be prone to spotting in heavy rain. The compact, bushy growth habit and light, typical tea fragrance make it a good choice for a mixed antique rose border or large container. Plant in full sun in well-drained, compost-enriched soil, and prune lightly in late winter, removing only dead or crowded wood to encourage vigorous new flowering canes.
sources: Help Me Find Roses — historical registry
The Old Rose Advisor (Brent C. Dickerson)
